title: An Ode to Counter-Positioning
gist: Counter-positioning — building a business model incumbents can't copy without damaging their own economics — is the one moat available to young startups before they can earn the other six of Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers, but it is inherently temporary and must be converted into durable moats (Scale Economies, Network Effects, Switching Costs) before an incumbent adapts or a new startup counter-positions against you.

insights.claim: Counter-positioning is defined (via Lindy CEO Flo Crivello) as developing a business model such that incumbents have conflicting incentives that prevent them from competing effectively — the incumbent's own advantages become the reason it can't respond.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Use this as a screen for startup moats: ask not 'is this better' but 'would copying this destroy the incumbent's existing profit pool or business model.'
insights.quote: the practice of developing your business model such that incumbents have conflicting incentives preventing them to compete effectively
insights.locator: In his primer on Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers

insights.claim: Counter-positioning is the one moat startups can wield before they are big enough to access the other six of Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers, because it turns an incumbent's own size and resources into the reason it can't compete.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: When evaluating an early-stage startup with no scale, network effects, or brand yet, counter-positioning is the moat to check for — it's the only one available at that stage.
insights.locator: There are 7 Powers, but if you made me choose a favorite

insights.claim: Counter-positioning is only a 'take-off phase' power — Hamilton Helmer himself calls it a partial source of power that must be converted into another, more durable moat before it fades, since it protects a startup from the specific incumbent it counter-positions against but not from other new startups.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Don't value a counter-positioned startup as if the advantage is permanent — check whether it is actively building a second, durable moat (scale, network effects, switching costs) during its window.
insights.quote: It’s the only one that’s a partial source of power. If you want real durability… you want to have another source of power.
insights.locator: As Hamilton [Helmer] would put it, counter-positioning is usually a take-off phase power

insights.claim: Being a better product is not the same as counter-positioning; real counter-positioning exists only when an incumbent can see that a challenger is better but genuinely cannot copy what makes it better without damaging the business it already has — otherwise 'better' is just a benefit, not a barrier.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Discount 'we're just better/faster' as a moat claim from founders — ask specifically what it would cost the incumbent, structurally, to copy the product.
insights.quote: Operational effectiveness means performing similar activities better than rivals perform them. Competitive strategy is about being different.
insights.locator: Being better is not counter positioning

themes.theme: Ramp's Spend-Less Model vs. Rewards Cards

insights.claim: Ramp counter-positioned against incumbent corporate card issuers by building its product around helping customers spend less, while incumbents were structurally locked into rewarding customers for spending more — because less customer spend meant less revenue for the incumbents and their shareholders, they could not copy Ramp's model without hurting their own business.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: When comparing fintech challengers to incumbents, check whether the challenger's core value prop actively conflicts with the incumbent's revenue model — that conflict, not product quality, is the durable edge.
insights.locator: If incumbent corporate cards incentivized customers to spend more

insights.claim: Two other corporate-card startups, Divvy and Brex, played the incumbents' own rewards/points game rather than counter-positioning, yet still exited well — Bill.com bought Divvy for $2.5 billion and Capital One bought Brex for $5.15 billion — while Ramp, which counter-positioned on spending less, is now valued at $44 billion.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The valuation gap ($2.5B/$5.15B exits vs. $44B standalone valuation) is a concrete data point that counter-positioning can compound into an order-of-magnitude larger outcome than playing an incumbent's game well.
insights.locator: Other startups like Divvy and Brex played the same game incumbents did

insights.claim: Base Power Company CEO Zach Dell argues that selling a better home battery at a discount invites incumbents to first copy the product and then cut price to run the challenger out of business ('your margin is my opportunity'), but selling electricity instead of the battery — where customers pay roughly 1/20th to 1/40th of the cost of owning the battery outright — forces incumbents to abandon their entire business model to respond, which is especially hard for a public company.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: In hardware-vs-service business model fights, watch whether a challenger sells the underlying asset-as-a-service rather than the asset itself — incumbents built around selling the asset face a structural, not just competitive, barrier to matching it.
insights.locator: Zach Dell’s conversation with David Senra

insights.claim: Base Power's counter-positioning advantage is temporary by design; the company will need to build other moats — Scale Economies, Cornered Resources, Switching Costs, Brand, and possibly Network Effects and Process Power — to protect its margins once incumbents eventually adapt their business models.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Track whether Base Power is visibly investing in scale/cornered-resource advantages now, since its current counter-positioning edge has an expiration date once incumbents can restructure.
insights.locator: Base won’t be able to use counter-positioning forever

themes.theme: Historical Playbook: Dell, Google, Amazon, Somos, Microsoft, Facebook

insights.claim: Dell counter-positioned against Compaq by selling direct to customers, since Compaq's dealer channel made direct sales painful for it to copy; once direct sales became universally adoptable, Dell's counter-positioning advantage disappeared, but by then Dell had used the window to build durable Scale Economies around its direct, just-in-time manufacturing model.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: This is the template case for 'convert your counter-positioning window into a scale-based moat before it closes' — a useful diligence question for any counter-positioned company.
insights.locator: Dell was counter-positioned against Compaq

insights.claim: Google could give Android away for free because its revenue came from search (more mobile usage meant more search revenue for Google), whereas Nokia had to monetize its mobile stack directly and would have killed its own business by matching Android's free price.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A useful test for AI/software competitive threats: ask whether the challenger monetizes in a completely different layer than the incumbent — that asymmetry, not capital alone, is what lets a challenger give something away that would bankrupt the incumbent to match.
insights.locator: When Google launched Android, it could afford to give it away for free

insights.claim: Amazon counter-positioned against Barnes & Noble because Amazon's direct-to-consumer fulfillment model was fundamentally incompatible with B&N's capital, culture, and profits built around physical stores — for B&N to match Amazon would have meant reallocating capital and executive attention away from its 'hugely profitable stores' toward a less profitable model.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The more capital and infrastructure an incumbent has sunk into its current model, the less able it is to adapt — a heuristic for judging which incumbents are actually vulnerable to a new entrant's model.
insights.quote: would be less profitable for them… versus the hugely profitable stores
insights.locator: Amazon, born on the internet, was built around direct-to-consumer fulfillment

insights.claim: Somos Internet counter-positioned against incumbent telcos by designing a new network architecture and building its own hardware; incumbent telcos can't respond because doing so would require ripping up billions of dollars of sunk CapEx spent on third-party hardware in the old configuration, most lack the in-house technical ability to re-architect their networks, and heavy debt loads used to finance existing buildouts prevent them from cutting prices to fight back.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A three-part checklist for evaluating whether an infrastructure incumbent can actually respond to a new entrant: sunk CapEx, in-house technical capability, and balance-sheet flexibility (debt load) to cut price.
insights.locator: My favorite example is Somos Internet

insights.claim: Microsoft beat IBM not by writing better software but by licensing DOS non-exclusively to as many PC makers as possible, deliberately commoditizing the hardware layer so it — not IBM's integrated hardware business — became the point of ecosystem integration; this is a 'vicious' form of counter-positioning where the entrant actively benefits from the destruction of the incumbent's profit pool, not merely tolerates cannibalizing it.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The strongest form of counter-positioning isn't just being unbothered by cannibalizing an incumbent's profit pool — it's actively profiting as that profit pool gets destroyed; look for this asymmetry when assessing platform-layer challengers.
insights.quote: free to become the whole point of integration for the entire ecosystem just by shipping bits
insights.locator: Microsoft didn’t win because it wrote better software than IBM

insights.claim: Facebook counter-positioned against MySpace (which reached 1 million users in February 2004, passed Friendster the next month, and quintupled to 5 million users by November 2004) by deliberately staying small and exclusive — seeding the network at Harvard and growing in small circles — a strategy MySpace's mass-growth model made it structurally unable to copy.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Deliberately constraining growth/exclusivity can itself be a counter-positioning move against a mass-growth incumbent, because the incumbent's whole strategy is optimized for scale, not density.
insights.locator: Then there’s Facebook, which faced off against MySpace

themes.theme: AI Assistant Wars: Instinct vs. Meta's Muse

insights.claim: Instinct is a better AI assistant product than what came before it, but 'being better is not counter-positioning' — because Meta can copy its model and product at no strategic cost to itself (only cash), since Meta already owns the user data needed to replicate the value proposition.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Do not price a 'best-in-class AI product' startup as if product quality alone is a moat against a data-rich incumbent that can copy it for free — check whether copying would cost the incumbent anything structurally.
insights.locator: Being better is not counter positioning

insights.claim: Instinct raised a $350 million Series B at a $2.5 billion valuation in late August 2026, with one theory being that the capital was meant to let it keep offering the product for free to outrun competitors while it transitions toward a transaction-fee business model.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A concrete funding/valuation marker for the AI-assistant category as of late August 2026 — useful as a comp when assessing rival assistant raises.
insights.locator: it raised a $350 million Series B at a $2.5 billion valuation

insights.claim: It's rumored that Meta and others offered a 10-figure sum to acquire Instinct, which turned the offer down; Meta responded within the same week by launching its own competing AI assistant, Muse, since building a clone cost Meta only money, which it has in abundance.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A rejected 10-figure buyout followed immediately by the acquirer building a direct clone is a live case study in how little protection 'better product' offers against a cash-rich incumbent with the missing data/distribution pieces.
insights.locator: It’s rumored that Meta (and others) even offered 10 figures for Instinct!

insights.claim: Meta's structural advantages make its Muse assistant a serious threat regardless of product quality: Meta already knows enough about users to solve the cold-start recommendation problem, can integrate Muse directly into WhatsApp, FB Marketplace, and Meta Ray-Bans, can run it in its own massive data centers, and gives each user what amounts to a real computer's worth of compute — advantages it can subsidize indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: When assessing whether an AI-native startup can survive a Meta clone, weight distribution/data/compute subsidy advantages far more heavily than head-to-head product review comparisons.
insights.quote: a real-deal computer, and Meta is offering that to everyone in the United States, and eventually the world. It’s pretty extraordinary!
insights.locator: Meta knows more about you than anyone

insights.claim: Not every Meta clone succeeds — Threads has not displaced Twitter (X) despite Meta's attempt to copy it, because Twitter had genuine Network Effects acting as a real moat, showing that an incumbent's resources alone don't guarantee a copy wins if the original has a durable moat of its own.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The Threads/Twitter precedent is the counter-example investors should weigh against the Muse/Instinct fear case — whether Instinct wins may hinge on whether it can build a comparable Network Effect moat in time.
insights.quote: Threads hasn’t cured my Twitter addiction. But Twitter had Network Effects. It was moated.
insights.locator: Now, Zuck has tried to copy or create new products before

insights.claim: Instinct launched a 'Trusted Person' network built on a new Instinct-to-Instinct communication protocol, letting users' assistants coordinate directly with those of their significant others, family, and friends — an explicit attempt to build Network Effects before Meta's Muse reaches scale; the outcome depends on whether Instinct built enough of a real network effect before users default to Muse.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Watch Instinct's Trusted Person adoption/engagement as the key leading indicator of whether its counter-positioning window converts into a durable Network Effects moat before Muse's distribution advantage takes over.
insights.locator: Just yesterday, they introduced a Trusted Person network

themes.theme: Moats Still Matter Even in the AI Boom

insights.claim: a16z partner Josh Elman argued that 'the new moats are the same as the old moats' and that every few years the industry falls in love with shiny new technology and forgets the basic physics of consumer software — a critique the author extends to business strategy broadly, not just consumer software.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Treat 'this AI cycle is different, moats don't apply' claims from founders and investors with skepticism — the author frames this as a recurring, historically discredited pattern, not a new insight.
insights.quote: The new moats are the same as the old moats. Every few years, we fall in love with shiny new tech and forget the basic physics of consumer software.
insights.locator: Earlier this week, a16z partner Josh Elman tweeted

insights.claim: Because AI now makes writing code fast and cheap, unmoated AI products are easier to copy than ever, even by an incumbent's own engineers without needing to acquire anyone — reinforcing rather than reducing the need for real moats despite the current narrative that speed and taste can substitute for strategy.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: AI-accelerated cloning raises the bar for what counts as defensible in this cycle — a product edge with no structural moat is now even more perishable than in prior tech cycles.
insights.quote: without moats, any good company will get copied, even if the humans have to do it themselves
insights.locator: it’s probably easier than ever to copy unmoated products now that AI can write the code

insights.claim: Large AI-era acquisitions — Nvidia's $12,930,300,000 purchase of Hugging Face and Cursor's reported $60 billion outcome with SpaceX — show sizable payoffs are possible for unmoated or hard-to-define-moat products, but the author warns that 'acquisition hope is not a strategy and better is not a moat,' since incumbents are currently paying up simply because AI is novel, not because these products are structurally defensible.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Don't underwrite an AI startup's valuation on the assumption of a lucrative incumbent acquisition — the author frames current high prices as a temporary, novelty-driven willingness to pay rather than a repeatable strategy.
insights.quote: acquisition hope is not a strategy and better is not a moat
insights.locator: We are in a period in which AI is so shiny and new
